stimulus.text: “I am for doing good to the poor, but I differ in opinion of the means. I think the best way of doing good to the poor, is not making them easy in poverty, but leading or driving them out of it.” The more public provisions were made for the poor, the less they provided for themselves.
stimulus.source_note: Benjamin Franklin, “On the Price of Corn and Management of the Poor” (1766), abridged. Public domain.

source: original; stimulus viewed before writing — Benjamin Franklin (1766), abridged, public domain.

books.section: A. Protestant Evangelicalism and Enlightenment Philosophy

primary_sources: Benjamin Franklin, “On the Price of Corn and Management of the Poor” (1766)

stem: What does Franklin's argument assume about human nature?

options.text: That people never change their conduct, whatever rewards or punishments they face
options.misconception: If conduct never changed, provisions would make no difference — but Franklin says provisions do change conduct.

options.text: That people are naturally lazy and cannot be helped
options.misconception: Franklin believes people can be led out of poverty — his argument is about the right means, not about hopelessness.

options.text: That the poor prefer public provisions to honest work
options.misconception: Franklin does not say the poor prefer provisions — he says provisions change what they do, which is a claim about incentives.

options.text: That people answer to incentives, so relief design shapes their conduct

rationales.D: Franklin's whole case rests on incentives: make relief easy and people provide less for themselves; make work pay and they provide more. The design of relief, not the goodness of the poor, decides the outcome.
rationales.A: If conduct never changed, Franklin's warning would be empty. His argument needs conduct that answers to rewards.
rationales.B: Franklin does not call people hopeless. He argues they can be led out of poverty by the right design of relief.
rationales.C: Preference is not Franklin's claim. His claim is that the design of relief changes conduct — an incentives argument.
rationales.general:
1. Find what Franklin's warning needs. Provisions change conduct — the more provided, the less the poor provide for themselves.
2. Name the assumption underneath. Conduct answers to incentives, so the design of relief shapes what people do.
3. Test the alternatives. Fixed conduct, hopeless laziness, and preference for handouts all miss the mechanism.
Remember: an argument about policy usually hides a claim about human nature — find the claim and the policy follows.
